en: Preface to the Genealogy of the Śākya Clan The ancient virtuous masters of the Śākya clan of Zhongnan Mountain have transmitted the following oral tradition:
taking the ancestral Buddhas as their teachers, they felt ashamed to examine the original lineage of the Buddha, yet they sought to perpetuate the teachings of the Śākya.
Regarding their lineage,
I have felt ashamed to seek out the origins of the Śākya clan;
what I have now recorded based on my own investigation is likely quite close to the historical record.
Since it is said that reforming customs is a matter of principle rather than empty rhetoric,
there was once, in the Southern Qi dynasty, the Vinaya Master Sengyou,
whose learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular traditions and whose conduct provided comprehensive guidance.
He compiled the *Śākyaputravaṃśa* (The Genealogy of Śākyamuni) in ten fascicles.
The citations of historical precedents and categories of phenomena are so profuse that they can surely provide a broad perspective for scholars of former generations.
This was not intended as a guide for later generations.
My years are now pressing toward autumn, and I am approaching the valley of sorrow;
yet, having repeatedly received encouragement, I have exerted myself to present this once more.
I shall briefly present five sections to open up three cycles of inquiry;
let those who contemplate the Dharma-seed of our own lineage examine this meaning in detail.
First, the introduction concerning the basis: the designation of the "Worthy Eon" (*bhadrakalpa*) refers to the reason for establishing its name based on the timing and destiny of one's lifespan.
Second, the sequence of the origins of the clan, which refers to the antiquity or recentness of obtaining the surname and whether its branches and roots are separate or joined.
Third, the sequence of the territory relied upon, which refers to the continent where one dwells and by what reasoning this is known.
The fourth sequence concerns the transformative manifestations of the Dharma King’s lineage, referring to the manner in which the Dharma Kings appear in the world to transform beings.
The fifth sequence concerns the descendants of the sages and ordinary beings, referring to how both the monastic and lay lineages flow far and wide without interruption.
1. Introduction on the Basis: Regarding the Initial Introduction on the Basis of the Bhadrakalpa.

Now, as for the opening of heaven and earth, it is the common parlance of worldly custom that the Great Primal Essence (*taisu*) and the Great Ease (*taiyi*), along with Yin and Yang, provide the covering and supporting of all things.
Examining it from antiquity to the present, nothing verifiable can be found;
entrusting it to the various schools, there is no lack of empty fabrications. Some say:
The heavens tilted toward the northwest and the earth gaped toward the southeast;
he refined the five stones to repair them from above and severed the legs of the giant turtle to support them from below.
Down to the time of Heaven, Earth, and the Human Sovereigns with their serpent bodies and ox-heads,
through the nine eras and four clans who acted as shepherds and rulers of men—
the paths of these beings were so muddled and complex that they are beyond the power of full description.
Now, relying on the authentic teachings, I shall fully enumerate the conditions of the kalpas.
What is the name of a *kalpa*?
In this language, it is translated as "time."
If one follows the Western Indian name, it is called *kalpa*;
in this land, it is translated as "Great Time.
This one Great Time consists of countless years.
It can only be understood in detail by means of an illustration.
A sutra says: "Suppose there were a great city, forty li square, filled to the brim with mustard seeds."
There are gods of long life who take one mustard seed from a city every three years; though the kalpa has already become empty, it is not yet exhausted.
There is also a stone forty li square;
if one brushes it once every three years, though the stone is worn away, the duration of the kalpa is not yet exhausted.
In this manner, kalpas succeed one another in an endless succession.
There are those with life who, through the four modes of birth, remain perpetually submerged and do not emerge.
This present kalpa is named Bhadra (the Auspicious).
At the beginning of the kalpa, when the great waters overflowed everywhere,
one thousand blue lotuses grew;
those in the fourth dhyāna heaven had previously witnessed these past events.
They then informed one another that in this world there were now a thousand Buddhas appearing;
thus, this period may be designated as the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Eon).
Therefore, a sutra states:
These are precisely the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Beginning with Krakucchanda as the first,
the last to attain Buddhahood is named Ruci.
Thus it is known that the first was Krakucchanda Tathāgata,
the second Kanakamuni,
the third Kāśyapa, and the fourth Śākyamuni.
The one we take as our teacher is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa.
According to the Hīnayāna sūtras, prior to the Bhadrakalpa,
the kalpa was empty and devoid of Buddhas.
During ninety-one kalpas, there was only Vipaśyin alone;
during thirty-four kalpas, three Buddhas appeared in the world;
together with the four Buddhas of the present Bhadrakalpa, these constitute seven.
As has been commonly taught,
according to the Mahāyāna sūtras, there are three thousand Buddhas throughout the three periods of the three kalpas.
The past was the Adorned Eon;
the present is named Worthy;
the future is the Constellations.
The three thousand princes attained Buddhahood in succession;
this arose from the differences in their perceptions caused by the clarity or obscurity of their mental understanding.
As they spread their teachings according to the capacities of beings, it is impossible to establish a fixed order among them.
Even at a single assembly on Vulture Peak, five thousand still withdrew;
the Great Emptiness of the *Prajñāpāramitā* contains those who have realized only the Lesser Fruit;
and rebirth in the Pure Land without extinction is reserved for those who have attained the stages of *bhūmi* and *vihāra*.
That this great fire has consumed all things truly pertains to those who have arisen and passed away; by means of this analogy, there is no need for doubt.
This kalpa is named Bhadra, signifying the manifestation of a thousand Buddhas.
One must know this.
2. Preface on the Origins of Clans and Surnames. Regarding the emergence of surnames and clans:
their original purpose was to summon forth one’s essential nature.
Therefore, names and forms are assigned according to the categories of things.
As for the origins of surnames in the Eastern Land (China), there were originally only nine;
thus it is said that they may derive from posthumous titles (*śi-hao*).
Examples include Tang, Yu, Wen, and Wu;
or those enfeoffed by rank,
such as the Marquis of Song and the Duke of Wei.
Sometimes they are derived from official titles,
such as Sima, Situ, Bo, Zhong, Shu, and Ji;
sometimes they are derived from places of residence, such as Guo, Yuan, Chi, and Chi.
Sometimes, due to specific affairs, there were the divinations of the sorceress of Mount Taoqiu;
sometimes, due to the holding of office, there were the "three crows" and "five deer.
In later generations, these followed various activities, spreading widely until they became increasingly ostentatious.
One need not labor over a detailed description of one's own physical appearance here and now.
Regarding the lineages of the Great Xia (China), there are four different types, namely: the Kṣatriya.
Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
The Kṣatriya royal lineage is the most noble,
having been transmitted without interruption since the beginning of the kalpa;
the other three castes are not discussed here.
This merely clarifies the Buddha’s clan, which is divided into five distinct categories:
first, Gautama;
second, Ikṣvāku.
The third is Śākya;
the fourth is Śāiya;
the fifth is Sūryavaṃśa (the Solar Lineage).
Regarding the term "Gautama," as stated in the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings*:
"In the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Bodhisattva..."
Originally a king,
he lost both his parents early in life and abdicated the throne to seek the Way.
His master’s surname was Gautama, and thus he adopted it as his own.
The term *Gautama* in the language of Tang is the name of a star.
Just as the Zhang clan established their surname based on a star,
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The clan name Nigodha has been transmitted from antiquity.
As for the term "Gautama," this is translated as "mud."

However, the translator has taken the words according to their common usage; I have now consulted a Brahmin monk, who says that *gautama* means "clay" or "mud," while *kaundinya* is the name of a star.
Therefore, we know that because he acquired his clan name from a star, it certainly cannot mean "mud."
Regarding the term "sugarcane," it is as stated in that sutra:
the Bodhisattva went into a sugarcane grove.
He wandered and dwelt while cultivating the Way;
he was named after the garden where he resided,
and is also called Ikṣvāku because of the sugarcane.
The *Buddhacarita* states that he was a descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was contemplating the Way within the garden.
Due to his past karma, he was captured by bandits and impaled upon a wooden stake,
with blood flowing onto the ground.
The Great Seer Gautama possesses pure divine vision.
After the Bodhisattva’s lineage was severed, there was no means for a Buddha to appear;
[the deity] flew from the mountain to mournfully enshroud the corpse,
taking the blood from within the earth and kneading it into a clay ball.
He placed them in two vessels and returned to his dwelling;
by the power of a divine mantra, after ten months had passed,
the one on the left transformed into a male and the one on the right transformed into a female.
The sage Gautama subsequently restored it.
Regarding the term "Śākya," as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: [text follows].
The Buddha was of the Śākya clan;
he is also called the Śākya Kingdom.
I have not yet ascertained the meaning of this name.
Regarding the term "Śākya," the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: In the past,
there was a king named Yima (Yi-mo), who was the tenth of the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) and lived one hundred lifetimes prior to the Buddha’s own life.
Regarding the banishment of the four sons, the fourth son, named Śobha, was ordered by King Śuddhodana to depart from the country.
Having received the king’s command, he arrived at the Northern Snow Mountains.
It is situated within a forest of straight trees.
According to the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya,
it lies to the north of the Snowy Mountains, vast and open on all four sides.
Vegetables and fruits flourished, and after several years had passed since he halted his carriage there,
people flocked to him like to a marketplace until it became a powerful state.
His father thought of summoning him back, but he declined on the grounds of his transgressions and did not return.
The father-king thrice sighed, "My son possesses such capability," and for this reason he was named Śākya.
As the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Events) says:
Dīpaṃkara Buddha said,
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
Śākya is "Capable of Writing" (Nengwen) and "Benevolent" (Ren).
According to the current Tang translation, it is the same as in the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Origin of the Lineage).
Therefore, these four sons took their names as their clan surnames based on these qualities.
However, the sūtra texts regarding the clan name of Śākya vary between singular and plural forms,
much like the usage of names such as Fang Shuo and Ma Qiong in this land [of China].
The Mahīśāsaka school says:
He dwelt in the Forest of Straight Trees,
and was also named Śāka.
Now, according to the Sanskrit pronunciation, "Shi" (釋) is called *Śākya*.
In India, various things and objects often have multiple names;
furthermore, this [clan name] was derived from the forest (*śāka-vana*) and thus used as a surname.
According to a separate tradition, there is a tree in that land called Śāka,
whose roots and trunk are lush and flourishing;
those skilled in physiognomy say:
They must have departed from their sovereign state;
consequently, the four sons established kingdoms and adopted clan names. Although this is not according to the formal teachings of the scriptures, it is recorded here as an eccentric account.
As for those said to be of Solar Descent:
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"The father's name was Riyue (Sun-Moon); the circumstances thereof are not yet detailed. It comprehensively clarifies that although there are five distinct branches, they share a single lineage;
these divisions arose due to the gradual evolution of practices according to specific circumstances.
However, the Śākya clan is extensively elucidated across many scriptures;
as for the others, they appear and disappear according to conditions and are cited accordingly.
Thus, Vinaya Master Sengyou said:
Looking up, we reflect that Dīpaṃkara bestowed a prophecy, designating him as Śākyamuni;
through this profound mandate and hidden resonance, he recorded the Śākya clan,
such that his name emerged even before form had taken shape.
Its traces manifest after [the Buddha] has passed into birth;
its radiance shines upon devas and humans throughout the succession of vast kalpas.
How profound is its source!
I have sought [the meaning of] Gautama as the father of one clan,
and Śākya as the mother of one clan;
therefore, the five men followed the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha is named Gautama;
this is clearly the logical principle by which a son inherits his father's clan name.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
The father's name was Sun;
his place of birth was named Śākya,
which clearly indicates the mother's clan.
The ancient seer Gautama took his blood and placed it in a vessel;
later, it transformed into a boy and a girl, from whom the Śākya lineage subsequently arose.
Examining the source, these two bodies were originally one blood that later divided into two forms.
Through marriage and the transformations of the womb, the branches have become extensive;
yet when speaking from the perspective of the fundamental, these truly overflow the bounds of ritual propriety.
When examining matters through their conditions, the great principles are fundamentally at odds.
Why is this? According to the records, the Śākya clan has long since severed all matrimonial ties with their kinsmen;
this darkly accords with the teachings established by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius in this land.
As a successor to the Wheel-Turning Kings, his prestige was high throughout the world;
when dividing the lineage and taking a bride, he would not intermarry with low-born clans.
It is reckoned that these two families share a common ancestor in the ancient seers.
The principle that fetal blood is no different [from one's own] makes it difficult to sever the logical precedent.
This is as with the surnames of the Eastern Xia (China),
most of which originally derive from the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
Now, as for the intermingling of marriages and unions, it is impossible to distinguish them or separate them.
Above, the origins of surnames were clarified;
now, the sources from which lineages arise are clarified.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
At the beginning of the formation of a great kalpa, when there were as yet no sun or moon,
the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their merit exhausted, descended to be born below.
They all transformed into human beings who took joy as their sustenance;
their bodies emitted light that shone afar, and they traveled through the air with ease.
Among them, there were no distinctions of male or female, nor of noble or humble, nor of kin and relatives.
The flavor of the natural earth was like clarified butter and honey.
Those who tasted it subsequently developed a craving for solid food;
when the radiance faded and their supernormal powers vanished, they cried out in lamentation upon the ground.
Those who ate much became haggard in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant in form;
thus, competition arose, and the *rasa* of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) vanished.
Furthermore, the skin of the earth (*pṛthivī-tvac*) appeared, and then the flesh of the earth (*pṛthivī-māṃsa*) appeared.
Because of the quantity of food consumed, various evils converged;
furthermore, as the fragrant rice became endowed with all excellent flavors,
those who were greedy for food came to possess both male and female sexual organs.
In this manner, they gradually became husband and wife,
and thus the birth from a womb first began.
According to the *Loutan jing*, there was naturally growing non-glutinous rice that ripened by evening after being harvested in the morning.
The *Zhonghan* states:
"The rice was four inches long, and people vied with one another to take it in advance.
They instructed each other in this manner."
Once the place where things are pre-empted has been reached, they no longer arise.
Master Yu said:
"When the corrupting winds have begun to stir, the pure source then fades away."
When spiritual beings communicate their resonance, even a thunderbolt strike becomes delayed.
I have humbly learned that during the days of the two Han dynasties,
when taxes were increased in Donglai, the sea fish swam away in secret depths.
When the tax was increased at Hepu, the pearl oysters moved far away;
thus, when the present compares with the ancient, it exceeds even the correspondence of a tally.
That non-glutinous rice does not grow there is not enough cause for surprise or doubt.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
At that time, when sentient beings saw that non-glutinous rice no longer grew spontaneously, they...
Each harbored grief and distress,
and they mutually demarcated their fields and houses to establish boundaries.
Consequently, there were those who hid their own rice and stole grain from the fields of others;
as this matter arose, no one was able to resolve it.
It was therefore deliberated that one person be appointed, titled the Lord of Equality.
He continued to reward the virtuous and punish the wicked, while providing for their needs.
At that time, there was a man of magnificent appearance and imposing presence,
whose dignified majesty inspired awe and whom the multitude trusted and obeyed.
They then collectively invited him;
once he had accepted, he was consequently given the title "Lord of Men" (Min-zhu).
The *Loutan jing* says:
The multitude said of themselves, "He shall be our leader," and they designated him as King (*rāja*).
Because he took the grain tribute, he was called *kṣatriya*; in the language of Tang, *kṣatriya* is translated as "landowner" (*tiandi zhǔ*).
Because there were disputes and litigations on each day of the initial division of the lands,
this Lord of Time was established; at that time, Jambudvīpa was wealthy, blissful, and peaceful,
and the earth produced green grass like the feathers of a peacock.
In more than eighty thousand kingdoms and villages, people could hear one another,
yet there were none afflicted by the sufferings of cold, heat, or disease;
the king governed with righteousness and practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
They revered one another like father and son.
The lifespan of humans was so exceedingly long that it could not be measured.
Later, there were other kings who did not practice the True Dharma.
Their lifespan subsequently decreased until it reached one hundred thousand years;
thus it gradually diminished until it reached the present century.
The above clarifies what preceded the Śākya clan.
At the beginning of the kalpa, he was the first to establish himself as king;
through successive generations, there arose the lineages of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and minor kings (*kṣudra-rāja*), continuing this succession.
The first king, a lord of men, was named Mahāpuruṣa. This is recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), while other accounts appear in the second chapter of the *Dīrgha-āgama*.

"Prince Tiṣya was named Piyaka.
There were five wheel-turning sage-kings."

These ten wheel-turning kings appear interchangeably in the Sūtras and Vinayas, and their enumeration is largely the same; however,
one must fear that there may be confusion between ordinary persons and sages.
Now, judging by the facts, it cannot be that there were eighty thousand [such rulers];
they must have been exclusively sage-emperors.
It can only be that the Ten Wheels are the correct [number].
The remaining descendants were ordinary people,
as clarified in the Vinaya;

The sutras collectively refer to them as "holy emperors" (shengdi).
This must certainly mean they are "holy" from the perspective of their fundamental nature;
however, from the perspective of their phenomenal flow, they are all subsumed under the category of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Furthermore, as stated in the tenth wheel:

Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The last king was named Mahāsammata;

Thus it has been verified from the very beginning of the universe.
The Creator fashioned and perfected all things, establishing the Imperial Ultimate;

down to the time of Shensi.

Since then, ten dynasties have flourished;
all were holy kings and were alike known as the Imperial lineage.
Those of the same lineage may follow the primary heir;
those of different branches may be divided.
None, however, fail to receive the Heavenly mandate.
Ruling over the entire world,
their long lineages and distant successors are difficult to fathom;
as for the various emperors of the Two Han dynasties, many were not the legitimate heirs.
The Wei, Jin, Song, and Qi dynasties were interconnected through successive lineages;
when one case is used as an analogy for another, the principle is naturally so.
Now, let us enumerate them from the beginning.
In total, there were eighty-four thousand two hundred and fifty-three kings;
subsequently, down to the first thirty-three kings prior to the Bodhisattva, they were merely like scattered grains.
Next was the lineage of the Ten Wheels.
Eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten.

This is the ancestral lineage of the Bodhisattvas.

the first was named Śuddhodana (the *Benqi jing* says "Pure White," while some sūtras simply refer to him as "Pure"); the second was named Śuklodana (the *Shier you jing* omits the character for "rice"); the same applies to the other two kings: the third was named Droṇodana, and the fourth was named Amṛtodana. Devadatta was born on the seventh day of the fourth month at the time of the morning meal;
he stood one zhang, five chi, and four cun tall and was the son of the second of the Buddha’s two paternal uncles.

Ānanda was born on the tenth day of the fourth month; his height was one zhang, five chi, and three cun. The Buddha’s paternal cousin was Devadatta. 3. Preface: The Regions Entrusted Now, the regions entrusted [by the Buddha] shall be determined by six principles: first, investigating the names; second, estimating the measurements; third, distinguishing the times; fourth, following the prevailing influence; fifth, relying on excellence; and sixth, examining the texts. 1. Investigating the Names I have heard: *The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions* (Taishō Tripiṭaka, Vol. 51, No. 2087) states: "In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma-treasury to Kāśyapa, and further charged him with the task of transmitting it to Ānanda. Subsequently, Ānanda transmitted it to Śānavāsika, and Śānavāsika transmitted it to Upagupta. Thus, from the Buddha down to Upagupta, there were four patriarchs who successively upheld the teachings. Furthermore, the *Record of the Western Regions* notes: "The Buddha entrusted the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākāśyapa entrusted it to Ānanda. the Buddha-dharma will remain in the world for ten thousand years;

the Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, Rāhula, and others.
The sixteen great arhats shall cause the Buddha-dharma to endure;
furthermore, ninety-nine billion other arhats personally received tally-sticks from before the Buddha’s presence,
vowing to maintain their lifespans and protect the Dharma without interruption.
Each of the great arhats has their own retinue;

residing in Jambudvīpa and the other three continents, as well as in the heavens, they act as fields of merit for beings and dwell there to protect the Dharma, and thus they do not observe the passage of time. Furthermore, according to another tradition:
Eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was a great arhat in the Kingdom of Siṃhala named Jayamitra.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he issued a broad summons to the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to Kāśyapa and, subsequently, to the sixteen great Arhats,
who dwell in the four continents and the heavens, maintaining their lives to protect the Dharma until the time when the human lifespan has decreased to ten years.

When the Kalpa of Swords arises, all the holy ones temporarily disappear; then, when the human lifespan increases back to one hundred years, the holy ones emerge en masse as before to transform and guide beings, once again manifesting their presence.
When the lifespan of the Perfect Being had increased to sixty thousand years,
all the sages assembled in Jambudvīpa and gathered together all the relics of the Tathāgata.
A great stūpa, adorned with the seven precious jewels,
arose and hovered in mid-air.
All the arhats prostrated before the Buddha’s stūpa and spoke these words:
We pay homage to all the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having received the Buddha’s final charge to protect and uphold the True Dharma,
we have now reached the end of our conditions and completed what was to be done.
Today we take our leave to enter nirvana;
then, by the power of our vows,
fire manifested in the sky and extinguished us, leaving no remains behind.
When the Tathāgata’s relics have vanished into the adamantine limit (*vajrakoṭi*),
at that time the names of the Triple Gem will cease to exist in this world.
This shall continue until the human lifespan reaches seventy thousand years.
Seventy trillion pratyekabuddhas appeared,
manifesting supernatural powers and transformations solely to serve as fields of merit for the world;
this continued until Maitreya descended at the age of eighty thousand years.
Based on this, the Buddha’s transformations are continuous from one period to the next.
My own Buddhist genealogy (*fǔ*) is different from the ordinary;
it follows the conventions of secular genealogical records.
The beginning arose from three and five;
in the middle flow, the branches diverged into many streams.
But for the Buddha, the beginning is without beginning.
It marks the dawn of seeking the Way during the Kaiyuan era;
in the end, it culminates in the infinite.
This clarifies that the conditions for transforming through the Way are inexhaustible.
Based on these words, it is said that the Śākyamuni Buddha’s propagation of the Dharma lasted for his full lifespan of sixty thousand years,
and the succession of the Pratyekabuddhas reached an auspicious period of one thousand *zhī* (chi).
Nevertheless, the Sūtras and Vinaya clarify that [the teachings] shall endure for a thousand or ten thousand years.

Judging by this standard, was his penetration not truly vast?
Furthermore, the clan name Śākya has both secular and monastic dimensions.
In its secular aspect, they still occupy royal positions,
such as the lords of Oḍra in Northern India and others.
The Way pervades the great chiliocosm and extends afar to the sixty thousand worlds;
like the creeping vines of the kudzu, it is interwoven and exists together with the Dharma.
Thus, though the Way covered the eastern lands, it was three times subjected to destruction and pruning.
Although it is said that this [teaching] perished while it still existed in other lands,
sixteen great sages and billions of *aśaikṣas* secretly protected and propagated it, and thus it was soon restored.
Thus, that which is extinguished cannot be extinguished; this is surely beyond human design.
That which can be expanded should be truly expanded, for its ultimate reliance is upon the power of the Sage.
One should simply depend upon the established teachings and follow their application in contemplative practice.
To suppress and subdue delusions and perversions, and to eliminate the defilements of karma—
if one exerts effort without ceasing, the completion of even a single basketful of earth may be expected;
yet to turn one's back on this and remain indolent is ultimately to come away empty-handed.
Therefore, at the end of this genealogy, I have issued these admonitions and composed this preface.
